title: Welcome to Kanji
goal: Understand what kanji are, why they are used, how kanji can be broken into smaller parts, and how Japanese readings work.

blocks.text: Welcome to the N5 Kanji Journey.
Our journey begins in **Hokkaido**, the northernmost of Japan's four main islands.
You will travel across Japan from north to south, learning Japanese through the places you visit.
But before we start learning lots of kanji, there is something important you need to understand:
What exactly is a kanji?
Japanese uses several writing systems. **ひらがな** and **カタカナ** are phonetic writing systems: their characters mainly represent sounds.
**{漢字|かんじ}**, on the other hand, are characters that carry meaning.
Kanji give us information about both **what something means** and, depending on the word, **how it is read**.
You don't need to memorize every kanji as a meaningless shape. Throughout this Journey, we will learn to look inside them.
Let's look at the name of the place we are visiting.
North + Sea + Way
blocks.title: Very literally

blocks.text: A kanji can have a meaning by itself, but its reading depends on the word it appears in.
blocks.title: First important lesson

blocks.text: We are going to see this again and again.

cards.title: Kanji Are Not Always One Sound

blocks.text: You may encounter this character with different readings. On its own it is **きた** (north):
But 北 can also have an **on'yomi** reading, **ホク**:
And in 北海道 the reading becomes **ほっ** rather than simply ほく:
Kanji readings are not always predictable from one simple rule.
blocks.title: Warning

blocks.text: We will learn useful patterns that help us make good guesses, but Japanese has exceptions and sound changes.
A kanji can have two broad types of readings.
Generally the Japanese reading tied to the character's native Japanese word. For 北, **きた** is a kun'yomi reading.
A reading that came from the historical adoption of Chinese pronunciations. For 北, **ホク** is an on'yomi reading.
A useful beginner pattern
In a compound word, **on'yomi is often used** (北部 → ほくぶ). As a native Japanese word, **kun'yomi is often used** (北 → きた).
These are useful patterns, but they are NOT absolute rules. Your goal is not to memorize a fake formula - it is to gradually get good at recognizing patterns.
blocks.title: Patterns, not rules

blocks.text: They may look complicated at first, but kanji are often made from smaller components.
These components can sometimes give us clues about:

items: meaning
pronunciation
category
shape
historical origin

blocks.text: This is where **radicals** become useful.
A **radical** is a component traditionally used to classify and index kanji. In learning, people often use the word more loosely for an important component inside a kanji.
Radical ≠ always 'the meaning of the kanji'
blocks.title: An important distinction

blocks.text: Sometimes a component gives a strong meaning clue. Sometimes it gives a pronunciation clue. Sometimes it mainly helps identify the character.
Don't think 'I know the radical, so I know the whole kanji.' Think: 'This part may give me a clue.'
It is a shortened form of 水, and you will see it in many kanji connected with water or liquid:
The component doesn't guarantee the meaning, but it gives a useful clue: 'This kanji may have something to do with water.'
You have already learned something that will be useful far beyond Hokkaido.
You will meet 辶 many times during your journey. For example:
Components are clues, not magic definitions.
The structure of 北 is different from 海 and 道. Its traditional radical is 匕, but this does **not** mean 匕 = north.
The ancient form showed people positioned back-to-back, and the character later came to mean 'north'.
Not every part of a kanji tells you its meaning.
blocks.title: Another important lesson

blocks.text: Understanding a kanji can mean learning:

items: its components
its history
its meaning
its readings
the words where it appears

blocks.text: We have arrived at our first city.
Sapporo is the capital and largest city of Hokkaido.
A place name may contain kanji that you haven't formally learned yet. 札 and 幌 are **encounter characters**: you have met them, and some will be studied properly later in your Journey.
blocks.title: That's okay

blocks.text: Now look inside {札幌|さっぽろ}.
Both parts of 札幌 carry a clue: 木 (wood) in 札 and 巾 (cloth) in 幌. Neither tells you how the name is read - that is something you simply meet and remember. Components are clues, not magic definitions.
Now let's use some of today's kanji.
Assisted location example: の means “of”; 北 means “north”; にあります means “is located in/at”. You will practice this pattern more fully in Asahikawa.
Now let's introduce the city.
Sapporo + topic + Hokkaido + の + town/city + です. の connects the place name to 町. This describes Sapporo as a city in Hokkaido; です alone does not express geographic location.
blocks.title: A small language note

blocks.text: You have already learned several important ideas.

items: 北 → north, 海 → sea, 道 → way
北 can be きた (kun'yomi) or ホク (on'yomi)
海 contains 氵, the water component
道 contains 辶, the movement / road component
You have already met 札幌, even though 札 and 幌 have not been fully studied

blocks.text: This is exactly how your Journey will work.
① Kanji carry meaning
② Kanji can have multiple readings
③ On'yomi and kun'yomi

items: 訓読み (kun'yomi): generally native Japanese readings
音読み (on'yomi): readings historically derived from Chinese pronunciations

blocks.text: These are patterns, not perfect rules.
④ Components can give clues

items: 海: 氵 = water component, a clue for water-related kanji
道: 辶 = movement / road component, a clue for movement and paths
北: its traditional radical is 匕, but that does not mean 匕 = north

blocks.text: ⑤ Place names contain kanji too
Some place-name kanji will be familiar. Others will be new. That's okay.
⑥ You don't have to memorize everything immediately
Your Journey distinguishes between:

items: 学習 - Studied: you have formally learned it
出会い - Encountered: you have seen it, but haven't fully studied it yet
未来 - Future: you haven't reached it yet

blocks.text: Seeing a future kanji is not a test. It is a preview.

completion.title: You have taken your first step.
